items.prompt: Which check reads source code without running the app?
choices: SAST
DAST
Fuzzing
items.explanation: SAST scans the code as text, so nothing needs to be deployed or running.

items.prompt: Which check attacks a running app from the outside?
choices: SAST
DAST
SCA
items.explanation: DAST sends requests at a live instance the way an outside stranger would.

items.prompt: What does SCA compare against published flaw lists?
choices: Your own source code and its comments
Your servers and their open ports
Your dependencies and versions
items.explanation: SCA looks at the packages you depend on, not at the code you wrote.

items.prompt: What does fuzzing feed into a program?
choices: Huge volumes of odd or malformed input
Only carefully written valid test cases
Copies of real customer records
items.explanation: Fuzzing tries large amounts of unexpected input and watches for crashes.

items.prompt: Who performs a pentest?
choices: An automated rule matcher in the pipeline
A permitted human trying to break in
A dependency updater that runs nightly
items.explanation: A pentest is a person reasoning like an attacker, under agreed rules.

items.prompt: In the lock story, reading the lock's plans is closest to which check?
choices: Fuzzing
A pentest
SAST
items.explanation: Reading plans inspects the design without touching the fitted door.

items.prompt: Which two checks need a running target?
choices: DAST and fuzzing
SAST and the recall check
Source code review
items.explanation: Both send real input at something that is running; SAST and SCA read text.

items.prompt: What is a bug bounty?
choices: A fixed block of a tester's paid time each year
An open, paid invitation to report real flaws
A rule that blocks merges on high findings
items.explanation: Outside researchers are rewarded for reporting genuine vulnerabilities.

items.prompt: A team can only afford checks that need no deployed app on each pull request. Which pair fits?
choices: SAST and SCA, which read source and dependency lists
DAST and fuzzing, which need a running instance to attack
A pentest and a bug bounty, which need a human to act
DAST and a pentest, which both probe the finished system
items.explanation: Source scanning and dependency checking need only text, so they can run on every change before any deployment exists.
items.reference:
Five checks, five views
plans: SAST reads source, app not running
door: DAST attacks the running app
recall list: SCA checks dependency versions
hammering: fuzzing feeds odd input in bulk
locksmith: a pentest is a human attacker
Why: each check looks at a different thing, so each sees a different set of flaws.
items.learnMore:
The five checks

SAST and SCA need only text, so they work before anything runs. DAST, fuzzing and a pentest need a running target. Matching the check to what it looks at tells you what it can report.

Common mistake

Treating DAST as a faster SAST. DAST never reads your code; it only sees how the running app responds.
items.reflection: Think of something you own that has a lock, a warranty and a user routine. Which of the five checks has an everyday version there, and which one has none?

items.prompt: Which description separates SCA from SAST most clearly?
choices: SCA runs only after release, SAST runs only during design review
SCA inspects the packages you install, SAST inspects code you wrote
SCA attacks a live server, SAST reads the server's response headers
SCA tests for crashes, SAST tests for stolen passwords in the code
items.explanation: Both are text-based, but they read different things: third-party versions against published lists versus your own lines.

items.prompt: A parser crashes on a request containing a stray percent sign. Which check is built to find this kind of failure?
choices: SCA, which compares package versions to published lists
SAST, which reads the parser's comments for warnings
Fuzzing, which sends large volumes of malformed input
A bug bounty, which pays for crashes on a fixed schedule
items.explanation: Fuzzing needs no idea what a normal request looks like; it simply tries odd input in bulk and records what breaks.

items.prompt: A tool flags harmless code. What is that called?
choices: A false negative
A true positive
A false positive
items.explanation: A flag on something harmless is a false positive.

items.prompt: A tool stays silent about a real flaw. What is that called?
choices: A false negative
A false positive
A silent pass
items.explanation: Silence about something real is a false negative.

items.prompt: What can a pattern-matching scanner recognize?
choices: Anything a reasonable user would call a mistake
Shapes it was built to look for
Rules the business never wrote down
items.explanation: A scanner only finds patterns that someone programmed into it.

items.prompt: Why is a human tester still needed?
choices: Scanners are legally banned from touching real systems
Humans can scan faster than any tool
Only a person can judge what the system should allow
items.explanation: Judging intent is the part no pattern-matcher does.

items.prompt: Which kind of flaw do scanners usually miss?
choices: A flaw in the shop's own rules
A password written into the code
A query built by gluing text
items.explanation: Rule flaws leave no suspicious shape for a scanner to match.

items.prompt: What is the practical answer for a small team?
choices: Daily human testing instead of automated checks
Cheap automated checks plus occasional human testing
Whichever single tool has the most rules
items.explanation: Layering gives breadth from tools and judgment from people.

items.prompt: Which is cheaper per run?
choices: A hired pentest team
A bug bounty programme
An automated scanner
items.explanation: A scanner is nearly free per run; people are expensive.

items.prompt: What does a clean scan mean?
choices: Nothing familiar matched
The system is proven safe
A human has approved it
items.explanation: A clean scan only reports that nothing familiar was matched.

items.prompt: All four automated checks pass, yet a stranger gets a refund by ordering a negative quantity. What explains the silence?
choices: The tools ran too early in the week to see the checkout
Automated checks only inspect cosmetic parts of an application
The refund code used a dependency that was not yet published
No tool has a pattern for a rule the business never enforced
items.explanation: Scanners match shapes; a missing positivity rule has no suspicious shape, so only intent-level reasoning exposes it.
items.reference:
Shapes versus intent
tool: matches shapes it already knows
human: asks what the system was meant to allow
false positive: flag on something harmless
false negative: silence about something real
Why: a tool compares against known patterns; only a person can compare behavior with intent.
items.learnMore:
Why layering wins

Cheap checks remove obvious bugs early so a human's limited time goes to what only a human can see. Neither layer alone covers both jobs.

Common mistake

Reading 'zero findings' as 'zero flaws'. It means nothing the tool knows how to recognize was present.
items.reflection: Name a kind of mistake in some other field that a checklist would never catch but an experienced person would. What does that person know that the checklist does not?

items.prompt: A scanner flags a query built from two fixed text constants. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is a false positive, because no outside input reaches it
It is a false negative, because the scanner stayed silent on it
It is a real flaw, because any concatenation is unsafe
It proves the scanner is broken and should be replaced
items.explanation: The shape matches the rule, but nothing an attacker controls reaches it, so the flag is a false positive.

items.prompt: A manager proposes dropping the human pentest because tools are cheaper. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Pentests are legally required in every shop
Tools cannot judge what the system should allow
Tools cannot read source code or dependency lists
A pentest is faster than any scanner run
items.explanation: The gap is in kind, not degree: cheaper shape-matching cannot substitute for reasoning about intent.

items.prompt: What does SCA structurally miss?
choices: Dependencies with published flaws
Flaws nobody has published yet
Outdated package versions
items.explanation: SCA compares against published lists, so unpublished flaws are invisible to it.

items.prompt: What does fuzzing structurally miss?
choices: A parser that hangs on odd input
A crash from an oversized value
Wrong output with no crash
items.explanation: A fuzzer notices crashes and hangs, not outputs that are merely incorrect.

items.prompt: What does SAST not see?
choices: Settings applied only at deploy time
A hardcoded password in the source files
A query built by gluing text
items.explanation: SAST reads source; deployed configuration is outside its view.

items.prompt: What can DAST never test?
choices: A missing response header
A path it never discovered
A verbose error message page
items.explanation: A scanner can only attack what it manages to find.

items.prompt: What limits a pentest?
choices: It cannot test anything running in production
It only finds flaws that scanners already found
Coverage is limited by the tester's time
items.explanation: Coverage depends on the tester's time and imagination.

items.prompt: Which check can spot a missing response header?
choices: DAST
SCA
Fuzzing
items.explanation: Headers appear in responses, which DAST inspects on a running app.

items.prompt: Which check finds a crash caused by malformed input?
choices: A bug bounty
Fuzzing
SCA
items.explanation: Fuzzing is built around feeding odd input and watching for failures.

items.prompt: What do all automated checks lack?
choices: Access to any kind of source code at all
The ability to run on a fixed schedule
Knowledge of what the system should do
items.explanation: Intent is not visible in code shapes or traffic shapes.

items.prompt: A fuzzer runs for hours with no crash, yet a discount code applies twice with no error. Why did the fuzzer stay silent?
choices: Fuzzers cannot send input that contains numbers or letters
The fuzzer was pointed at the dependencies instead of the application
A double discount is not a crash, and fuzzing watches for crashes
Discount codes are always checked by the SCA step first
items.explanation: Fuzzing reports crashes and hangs; wrong-but-smooth behavior produces neither.
items.reference:
What each check cannot see
SAST: runtime settings, rules that look fine as text
DAST: paths it never found, intent-level rules
SCA: flaws nobody has published yet
fuzzing: wrong behavior that never crashes
pentest: anything the tester did not try
Why: each blind spot is some version of not knowing what the system was supposed to do.
items.learnMore:
Structural blind spots

A blind spot is built into what the check observes. SCA only sees version numbers, so a brand-new flaw is invisible to it until someone publishes it. Better rulesets shrink gaps; they do not remove them.

Common mistake

Assuming the blind spot is a maturity problem. It is a consequence of what the check looks at.
items.reflection: Pick a safety check you rely on in everyday life, such as a smoke alarm. What can it never detect, and what do you do instead for that case?

items.prompt: A flaw in a library is published today. Last week's SCA run was clean. What best explains this?
choices: SCA only checks libraries released before the current year
SCA skips any library that the code actually uses
A clean run proved the library had no flaws then or later
The list SCA compares against lacked that flaw last week
items.explanation: SCA compares versions to what is published at scan time; a later disclosure needs a fresh scan.

items.prompt: DAST reports nothing, but a hidden admin page reachable only by typing its address is exposed. Why was it missed?
choices: The scanner never found that path, so it never attacked it
DAST only tests pages that contain forms asking for passwords
The admin page used a framework that DAST cannot parse
Hidden pages are always covered by the SAST step
items.explanation: DAST attacks what it finds by crawling; an unlinked page is outside what it discovered.

items.prompt: A debug option is switched on in the deployed server's settings file but nowhere in the repository. Which check is least likely to see it?
choices: DAST, which can observe verbose responses from the live app
SAST, which reads source and not the deployed settings
A pentest, which can inspect the running configuration
A bug bounty, which attracts reports about leaked detail
items.explanation: SAST only sees what is in the repository; a setting applied at deploy time lives outside that view.

items.prompt: Which checks run on every pull request?
choices: A pentest and a bounty
SAST and SCA
DAST and fuzzing only
items.explanation: They need only text, so they are cheap enough to run on every change.

items.prompt: Why can't DAST run on every keystroke?
choices: It only works on code written many years ago
It refuses to read source code files
It needs a deployed, running app to attack
items.explanation: DAST needs something running, which makes each run slower and costlier.

items.prompt: How often does a scheduled pentest run?
choices: Periodically, e.g. yearly
On every single pull request
Every few seconds of the day
items.explanation: A person's time is costly, so engagements are scheduled.

items.prompt: Which check is cheapest per run?
choices: A pentest
SAST
A bounty
items.explanation: Reading source text costs almost nothing per run.

items.prompt: Why does a bug cost more the later it is caught?
choices: Later bugs are always larger in size
Tools charge extra after release
More rework built on top of it
items.explanation: Code piles up on the bug, and live users may be affected.

items.prompt: In the demo, what does each stage a bug survives do to the cost?
choices: Multiplies it by an assumed factor of ten
Adds an assumed fixed amount of ten per stage
Leaves it exactly as it was before
items.explanation: The factor is an illustrative assumption, not a measured figure.

items.prompt: Where does a bug bounty sit in the pipeline?
choices: Before the first commit
Always on, after release
Only during the build step
items.explanation: A standing offer, so reports can arrive at any time.

items.prompt: Which check fits the staging stage?
choices: SCA
A bug bounty
DAST
items.explanation: Staging is the first place a running copy of the app exists to be attacked.

items.prompt: In the demo, a bug with a base cost of 10 survives three stages. At the assumed factor of ten per stage, what is the cost?
items.explanation: The cost is 10 multiplied by ten three times, which is 10,000; the factor is an assumption of the demo.
items.reference:
Where each check runs
every change: SAST + SCA (text only, cheap)
every release: DAST + fuzzing (needs a running app)
scheduled: pentest (human, costly)
always on: bug bounty (after release)
Why: the more a check sees, the more each run costs, so it runs less often.
items.learnMore:
Cost, speed, and depth

These are one trade-off. Cheap checks run constantly and catch early bugs; costly ones run rarely and catch what the cheap ones cannot. The demo uses an assumed factor of ten per stage to show cost compounding.

Common mistake

Quoting the factor of ten as a measured fact. In this unit it is an illustrative assumption.
items.reflection: Think of a project in any field where a mistake found late was far more costly than one found early. What did the early version of the check look like?

items.prompt: A team wants DAST to run on every commit. What is the real obstacle?
choices: DAST cannot read any file that is stored in version control
DAST only works on applications written before the year 2000
A single run of DAST uses up the monthly scanner licence
Each run needs a deployed running copy, which costs time
items.explanation: Unlike text scanners, DAST needs something live to attack, so per-commit runs multiply deployment cost.

items.prompt: Which ordering matches cheapest-and-earliest to costliest-and-latest?
choices: SAST and SCA, then DAST and fuzzing, then a scheduled pentest
A scheduled pentest, then DAST and fuzzing, then SAST and SCA
DAST and fuzzing, then SAST and SCA, then a scheduled pentest
SCA, then a scheduled pentest, then SAST and DAST
items.explanation: Checks needing only text run first and often; ones needing a running app come later; people come last.

items.prompt: A scanner flags a query built from two fixed constants. What is it?
choices: A false positive
A false negative
A critical bug
items.explanation: No outside input reaches the line, so the flag is noise.

items.prompt: What is the first triage question about a flagged line?
choices: How old is the file it is in?
Can untrusted input reach it?
Who last edited that line?
items.explanation: Reachability decides whether the shape is actually dangerous.

items.prompt: How should a confirmed false positive be handled?
choices: Delete the scanner rule entirely for everyone
Ignore every future report
Suppress that line with a written reason
items.explanation: A reviewed suppression silences one line while keeping the rule.

items.prompt: Why not weaken the rule to stop a false positive?
choices: It would also hide real bugs of that shape
Rules cannot be changed after they are written
Weaker rules make scans run slower
items.explanation: The real finding shares the shape the rule matches.

items.prompt: A flagged dependency's flawed feature is never called. What is it?
choices: Certainly harmless forever
Real but possibly lower priority
Always the single most urgent finding
items.explanation: Reachability affects priority, though upgrading is usually cheap anyway.

items.prompt: Which worked-example finding had no tool pattern?
choices: The string-built search query
The missing response header
The negative quantity refund
items.explanation: Only the human tester found the rule flaw.

items.prompt: How does a fixed query keep the visitor's text safe?
choices: The text travels separately as data
The text is deleted before it is used
The query is longer than before
items.explanation: A parameterised query never reads the text as part of its structure.

items.prompt: Who confirms a fix really closes a finding?
choices: Whoever filed the ticket
The finder retests it
The scanner's vendor
items.explanation: A retest checks the fix actually works, not just that a ticket closed.

items.prompt: Two flags use the same rule. One joins a page request's text into a query; the other joins two fixed constants. How should they be triaged?
choices: Both are real because both of them match the rule's shape
The first is likely real and the second a false positive
Both are noise because the rule is the same one
The second is critical and the first can wait
items.explanation: Reachability separates them: visitor-controlled text reaches the first, nothing external reaches the second.
items.reference:
Is this finding real?
1. can untrusted input reach this line?
2. what is the worst outcome if it does?
no reach: false positive, suppress with a note
reach: real, score the severity
Why: a flag is a lead, not a verdict; triage turns it into a decision.
items.learnMore:
Triage before fixing

A scanner flags a shape. You decide whether the shape is dangerous here. A suppression with a reason fixes one noisy line; loosening the whole rule would also hide real bugs with the same shape.

Common mistake

Weakening a rule to remove one false positive. The same change silences the real finding too.
items.reflection: Think of an alarm in your life that goes off more often than it should. How would you decide which ring to ignore without disabling the alarm entirely?

items.prompt: SCA flags a library with a published flaw in an image-resizing feature the shop never calls. What is the best next step?
choices: Ignore it forever because the feature is unused
Declare it critical and halt all work today
Confirm the code never reaches it, then still schedule an upgrade
Remove the scanner so the flag stops appearing
items.explanation: Reachability lowers urgency, but an unused flaw can become used later, so a low-priority upgrade is sensible.

Keep it but never read its reports again
Switch to a different rule that matches nothing
Suppress reviewed lines and keep the rule active
items.explanation: Suppressions fix individual noisy lines; disabling would let the real bug with the same shape through.

The text is encrypted before it reaches the database
The database refuses any text containing quote marks
Parameters make the query run before the text arrives
items.explanation: Keeping text and structure apart means nothing in the text can change what the query does.

items.prompt: What decides a finding's severity?
choices: Impact and ease of exploitation
Which of the tools found it first
How long the report is
items.explanation: Severity measures how bad and how easy, not who found it.

items.prompt: Does the stage that found a bug set its severity?
choices: Yes, always
No
Only for pentests
items.explanation: Severity is a property of the bug itself.

items.prompt: What does a remediation deadline state?
choices: How long the scan took to run in total
When the tool was first installed
How fast a scored finding is fixed
items.explanation: Deadlines attach to severity after scoring.

items.prompt: What happens if the gate blocks on every finding?
choices: People start ignoring the bot
Every bug is fixed within a day
The scanner becomes faster
items.explanation: Too many minor blocks teach people to bypass the gate.

items.prompt: What happens if the gate blocks on nothing?
choices: Every bug gets found much earlier
The scanner becomes decoration
The build becomes slower
items.explanation: A gate that never blocks changes no behavior.

items.prompt: What is a common gate compromise?
choices: Block only on cosmetic style issues
Block every second merge at random
Block high only, ticket the rest
items.explanation: Serious findings stop the merge; minor ones are tracked.

items.prompt: Where would 'anyone can extract money' be scored?
choices: Critical
Low
Informational
items.explanation: Easy exploitation plus direct financial loss is the top tier.

items.prompt: Are 7, 30 and 90 days a universal standard?
choices: Yes, set by law
No, they are an example policy
Yes, set by every scanner vendor
items.explanation: Each organisation sets its own deadlines.

items.prompt: A pentest finds a refund bug usable by any visitor; a staging scan finds a missing header that needs a tricked victim. Which deadline order is sensible?
choices: The header is due first because the scan found it earlier
The refund bug is due first, the header later
Both share one deadline since both are real findings
The header is due first because it is easier to fix
items.explanation: Impact and ease of exploitation set urgency, and the refund bug is both severe and direct.

From score to action
critical: anyone can extract money
high: visitor text reaches the database
medium: missing header, needs a tricked victim
gate: block high and above, ticket the rest
Why: severity comes from impact and ease of exploitation, not from which check found it.

Scoring and gating

Scoring every finding on one scale makes 'critical' mean the same thing everywhere. The 7, 30 and 90 day deadlines in this unit are an example policy; each organisation chooses its own.

Common mistake

Setting urgency by the tool that found the bug. A slow human can find a critical flaw; a fast scanner can find a minor one.

choices: The codebase has no remaining findings of any severity
Pentests become unnecessary because the gate covers every possible flaw
Developers start bypassing the gate because it blocks constantly
The scanner runs faster because findings are blocked early
items.explanation: A gate that blocks on noise stops being trusted, which defeats its purpose.

items.prompt: What does scope define in a pentest?
choices: How long the report must be
Which tools the vendor sells
Which systems are in bounds
items.explanation: Scope names what may be tested and what may not.

items.prompt: What do rules of engagement define?
choices: What actions the tester may take
Which dependencies are installed
How many findings are due
items.explanation: They set limits such as no denial-of-service or staging only.

items.prompt: Why is the agreement written first?
choices: Reports are far easier to format that way
Permission turns an attack into a test
It makes scanners run faster
items.explanation: Without it the same actions may be unauthorised.

items.prompt: What does a retest confirm?
choices: The ticket has been created and filed
The tester was paid correctly
The fix really closes the finding
items.explanation: A closed ticket is not proof; a retest is.

items.prompt: How does a bug bounty differ from a pentest?
choices: It is always on, not time-boxed
It uses only automated scanners
It runs once, before release
items.explanation: Researchers can report at any time, whereas a pentest has fixed dates.

items.prompt: Why name an emergency contact?
choices: To thank the tester afterwards
In case something breaks mid-test
To choose a name for the final report
items.explanation: A live test can disturb a real system and someone must be reachable.

items.prompt: A tester finds a flaw outside the scope. What should they do?
choices: Keep testing it quietly
Publish it so others can see
Stop and report it
items.explanation: Outside scope there is no permission to continue.

items.prompt: Why use one severity scale in every report?
choices: So labels mean the same each time
So that the reports look much longer
So that the tester earns a bonus pay
items.explanation: A shared scale makes findings comparable.

items.prompt: A tester finds a flaw on a server not named in the agreement. What is the correct move?
choices: Stop, report to the named contact, and wait for scope to change
Continue testing it since the flaw is real and serious
Publish the flaw so the owner is under pressure to act fast
Test it only at night so nobody notices the change
items.explanation: Scope is the permission boundary; a real flaw does not extend it.
items.reference:
Agreed before the first test
scope: which systems are in bounds
rules: what actions are allowed
timeline: dates and an emergency contact
severity scale + remediation terms
retest: finder confirms each fix
Why: written permission is what turns an attack into a test.
items.learnMore:
Inside an engagement

A pentest is permitted, time-boxed and bounded. Scope and rules protect both sides. A bug bounty is the always-on cousin: continuous attention, but no promise that any given part is examined.

Common mistake

Treating a bounty as a replacement for a scheduled pentest. Coverage in a bounty is opportunistic, not guaranteed.
items.reflection: Imagine lending your house to a safety inspector for a day. What would you want written down first about where they may go and what they may do?

items.prompt: A company runs a bug bounty and asks whether it can drop its scheduled pentest. What is the strongest reply?
choices: Yes, because a bounty always covers every part of the system
No, because a bounty gives no guarantee any area is examined
Yes, because bounty hunters are bound by an agreed timeline
No, because bounties are limited to automated scanners
items.explanation: Bounty coverage depends on what researchers choose to try; a pentest is planned to cover chosen areas.

They proceed but delete the evidence afterwards
They ask for the rules to be changed in writing before testing live
They test live only on days when traffic is low

items.prompt: A ticket for a pentest finding is marked done, but the retest still reproduces the problem. What does that mean?

The tester made an error and the retest result is ignored
The finding is downgraded since it was already worked on
The finding stays open and the fix goes back for rework
items.explanation: The retest is the check on the fix; a failing retest overrides the ticket status.
